--- title: Draw your assumptions before drawing your conclusions 🔀 subtitle: Causal thinking with DAGs --forks, chains and colliders, simulated author: "Nelson Amaya" description: "Correlation is not causation --but why, exactly? Learn the three atoms of causal structure (fork, chain, collider), draw them as DAGs, and simulate each one to see when adjusting for a variable fixes an estimate and when it manufactures bias out of nothing." categories: - statistics - causality - DAG - ggdag - simulation date: "2026-07-04" date-modified: last-modified order: 4 level: Advanced duration: 45 min track: Think with data prerequisites: "All models are wrong" image: causal.png editor_options: chunk_output_type: console citation: url: https://nelsonamayad.github.io/R4DEV/sessions_thinking/04-causal/04-causal --- > *"No causes in; no causes out."*
--Nancy Cartwright ::: {.lesson-info} **Level:** Advanced  ·  **Time:** ~45 min  ·  **Prerequisites:** All models are wrong  ·  **Tools:** ggdag, dplyr, interactive OJS explainers (no installation needed) ::: ## You will learn to - Draw a causal diagram (DAG) and identify its three basic atoms: fork, chain, collider. - Simulate a confounder and see adjusting for it fix a biased estimate. - Simulate a collider and see adjusting for it *create* bias that wasn't there. - Ask a DAG which variables to adjust for with `ggdag_adjustment_set()`. ## PART I: The question regression can't answer alone The [previous session](/sessions_thinking/03-regression/03-regression.qmd) ended on a warning: a regression coefficient describes an *association*. But the questions worth money and lives are about **intervention**: what happens to sales *if* we cut the price? To health *if* we take the drug? Association answers "what do I see?"; causation answers "what if I act?" --and no formula converts one into the other[^1]. [^1]: This is Judea Pearl's "ladder of causation", from [*The Book of Why*](http://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/WHY/) --the best non-technical entry to this whole subject. [^hernan]: It is the subtitle of Hernán's free HarvardX course [*Causal Diagrams: Draw Your Assumptions Before Your Conclusions*](https://www.edx.org/learn/data-analysis/harvard-university-causal-diagrams-draw-your-assumptions-before-your-conclusions), and the working philosophy of the book he co-wrote with James Robins, [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatif) --free, rigorous, and the standard reference once you outgrow this session. What *does* convert one into the other is an ingredient statistics cannot supply: **your assumptions about how the world works**. This session's title is Miguel Hernán's motto[^hernan], and it is the whole method in one sentence. The modern discipline is to draw those assumptions as a graph --a **DAG** (directed acyclic graph): variables as nodes, arrows meaning "causes", no cycles allowed. Once drawn, the graph tells you --mechanically-- which variables you must adjust for and, just as important, which ones you must **leave alone**. Every causal structure, however monstrous, is built from three atoms. Let's draw them with [`ggdag`](https://r-causal.github.io/ggdag/) and then --this track's signature move-- *simulate each one* to see what it does to a regression. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(ggdag) fork <- ggdag::dagify(x ~ z, y ~ z, coords = ggdag::time_ordered_coords()) chain <- ggdag::dagify(m ~ x, y ~ m, coords = ggdag::time_ordered_coords()) collider <- ggdag::dagify(c ~ x, c ~ y, coords = ggdag::time_ordered_coords()) list(Fork = fork, Chain = chain, Collider = collider) |> purrr::imap(\(dag, name) { ggdag::ggdag(dag, node_size = 14, text_size = 4) + ggdag::theme_dag() + labs(title = name) }) |> patchwork::wrap_plots(nrow = 1) # <1> ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](04-causal_files/figure-html/4.atoms-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 1. `patchwork` glues the three plots side by side. Fork: `z` causes both `x` and `y`. Chain: `x` causes `y` *through* `m`. Collider: `x` and `y` *both cause* `c` --the arrows collide. ## PART II: The fork --confounding, the classic villain Ice cream sales correlate with drowning deaths. The fork explains it: summer (`z`) causes both. In a fork, `x` and `y` correlate **without any arrow between them** --and the fix is to *adjust* for the confounder. Here is the atom wearing its story: ```{ojs} //| echo: false drawDAG({ id: "dag-fork", w: 340, h: 155, nodes: [ {id: "Z", x: 170, y: 35, label: "summer"}, {id: "X", x: 60, y: 115, label: "ice cream"}, {id: "Y", x: 285, y: 115, label: "drownings"} ], edges: [ {from: "Z", to: "X"}, {from: "Z", to: "Y"}, {from: "X", to: "Y", color: C.ghost, dashed: true, opacity: 0.65, label: "no arrow --yet they correlate", ly: 18} ] }) ``` Now watch it in twelve lines: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(44) fork_world <- tibble( summer = rbinom(2000, 1, 0.5), # <1> ice_cream = 10 + 5 * summer + rnorm(2000), # <2> drownings = 2 + 3 * summer + rnorm(2000) # <3> ) lm(drownings ~ ice_cream, data = fork_world) |> broom::tidy() |> dplyr::filter(term == "ice_cream") # <4> lm(drownings ~ ice_cream + summer, data = fork_world) |> broom::tidy() |> dplyr::filter(term == "ice_cream") # <5> ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 ice_cream 0.517 0.00947 54.6 0 # A tibble: 1 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 ice_cream 0.00289 0.0223 0.130 0.897 ``` ::: ::: 1. A coin flip: is it summer? 2. Ice cream depends on summer --note it does **not** depend on drownings. 3. Drownings depend on summer --and **not** on ice cream. We built this world; we *know* the true effect of ice cream on drowning is exactly zero. 4. The naive regression finds a strong, "significant" effect. It is pure confounding. 5. Adjust for the fork and the coefficient collapses to ~0 --the truth we wired in. Adjustment worked because the graph said it would. This is the trap behind most "X linked to Y" headlines: wine drinkers live longer (income is the fork), private schools outperform (parental resources), coffee "causes" whatever it causes this week. The knee-jerk fix --"control for everything!"-- seems to follow. It doesn't. Meet the atom that punishes it. ## PART III: The collider --where adjusting *creates* bias In a collider, `x` and `y` are truly independent, but both cause `c`. Leave `c` alone and all is well. **Adjust for it --or select your sample on it-- and you manufacture a correlation out of nothing.** The classic example: are good-looking actors less talented? Suppose looks and talent are utterly unrelated, but either gets you into Hollywood: ```{ojs} //| echo: false drawDAG({ id: "dag-coll2", w: 340, h: 160, nodes: [ {id: "X", x: 60, y: 45, label: "looks"}, {id: "Y", x: 285, y: 45, label: "talent"}, {id: "C", x: 170, y: 125, label: "famous --the collider"} ], edges: [ {from: "X", to: "C"}, {from: "Y", to: "C"}, {from: "X", to: "Y", color: C.danger, dashed: true, opacity: 0.6, bend: -34, label: "manufactured by selecting on C", ly: -10} ] }) ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(44) hollywood <- tibble( looks = rnorm(5000), talent = rnorm(5000), # <1> famous = (looks + talent + rnorm(5000, sd = 0.5)) > 1.5 # <2> ) lm(talent ~ looks, data = hollywood) |> broom::tidy() |> dplyr::filter(term == "looks") # <3> lm(talent ~ looks, data = dplyr::filter(hollywood, famous)) |> broom::tidy() |> dplyr::filter(term == "looks") # <4> ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 looks -0.0162 0.0141 -1.15 0.251 # A tibble: 1 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 looks -0.592 0.0303 -19.6 3.14e-69 ``` ::: ::: 1. Independent by construction: the correlation between looks and talent is zero in this world. 2. Fame is the collider: you get in on looks, talent, or luck. 3. In the full population: no relationship, correctly. 4. Among the famous only: a strong *negative* effect appears from thin air. Among people who cleared the bar, being gorgeous means you *needed* less talent to get in --selection did the distorting, no villain required. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hollywood |> ggplot(aes(looks, talent, color = famous)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) + scale_color_manual(values = c("grey70", "#F75431")) + labs( title = "Collider bias, a.k.a. Berkson's paradox", subtitle = "No relationship in the population (grey). A strong negative one among the selected (orange).", color = "Famous" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](04-causal_files/figure-html/4.collider-plot-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: This is not a curiosity --it is everywhere your data was *filtered before you got it*: hospital patients (admission is a collider), survey respondents (responding is), hired employees, published papers, surviving companies. If your dataset exists because its rows cleared a bar, Berkson is already in it. ::: callout-note ## You've seen these before, animated The interactive explainers in [session 5 of the workshop](/sessions_workshop/05-animate/05-animate.qmd) let you *drag* the strength of a collider and an omitted variable and watch the bias move. This session is the theory those toys were built on. The chain (`x → m → y`), the third atom, gets an exercise below: adjusting for a **mediator** blocks the very effect you're trying to measure --a third distinct way "controlling for more" backfires. ```{ojs} //| echo: false drawDAG({ id: "dag-chain2", w: 340, h: 130, nodes: [ {id: "X", x: 60, y: 60, label: "education"}, {id: "M", x: 170, y: 60, label: "skill --the mediator"}, {id: "Y", x: 285, y: 60, label: "wages"} ], edges: [ {from: "X", to: "M"}, {from: "M", to: "Y"}, {from: "X", to: "Y", color: C.ghost, dashed: true, opacity: 0.65, bend: 40, label: "the whole effect travels through M --adjust for M and you block it", ly: 18} ] }) ``` ::: The moral of the two experiments, and arguably of the whole causal revolution: **whether to adjust for a variable is not a statistical question**. The same `+ z` in your formula is the cure in a fork and the poison in a collider --and only the DAG, i.e. your drawn assumptions, can tell you which world you're in[^2]. [^2]: `ggdag::ggdag_adjustment_set(dag, exposure = "x", outcome = "y")` automates the deduction: give it your graph and it returns the set(s) of variables to adjust for. The graph is your responsibility; the graph-reading is mechanical. So adjustment, guided by a DAG, can fix a confounded estimate --but only if the DAG is right, and nothing in the data can prove that it is. The next lesson, [Earning the arrow](/sessions_thinking/05-designs/05-designs.qmd), takes the other road: research designs that make the arrows you need true *by construction*, or at least make the ones you assume away visible. ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| output: false C = ({treat: "#F75431", ctrl: "#0E8CA8", ghost: "#8A979C", danger: "#D7263D"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| output: false drawDAG = ({id, w = 340, h = 170, nodes, edges}) => { const R = 17; const N = new Map(nodes.map(d => [d.id, d])); const parts = edges .filter(e => (e.opacity ?? 1) > 0.03) .map((e, i) => { const s = N.get(e.from), t = N.get(e.to); const rs = s.hidden ? 2 : R + 3, rt = t.hidden ? 2 : R + 8; const dx = t.x - s.x, dy = t.y - s.y, L = Math.hypot(dx, dy); const ux = dx / L, uy = dy / L; const x1 = s.x + ux * rs, y1 = s.y + uy * rs; const x2 = t.x - ux * rt, y2 = t.y - uy * rt; const bend = e.bend ?? 0; const cx = (x1 + x2) / 2 - uy * bend, cy = (y1 + y2) / 2 + ux * bend; const mid = {x: (x1 + 2 * cx + x2) / 4, y: (y1 + 2 * cy + y2) / 4}; const col = e.color ?? "currentColor"; return htl.svg` ${e.label ? htl.svg`${e.label}` : null} `; }); const dots = nodes.filter(n => !n.hidden).map(n => htl.svg` ${n.id} ${n.label ? htl.svg`${n.label}` : null} `); return htl.svg``; } ``` ## 🏗 Practice 4: Draw it, then simulate it {.unnumbered} All of these are a few lines of R --or a DAG you draw first and check with `ggdag` second. ::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"} # Basic - Simulate the third atom, the chain: `x` causes `m` (`m = 2*x + noise`), `m` causes `y` (`y = 3*m + noise`). Regress `y ~ x`, then `y ~ x + m`. The total effect of `x` is 6 --which regression finds it, and what does the other one estimate instead? - Draw last week's news. Take one "X linked to Y" headline, draw a DAG with at least one plausible fork, and use `ggdag_adjustment_set()` to state what the study would need to have adjusted for. ::: ::: {.callout-important icon="false" collapse="true"} # Intermediate - Break the fork fix: in the ice-cream world, adjust for a *noisy* version of summer (`summer_reported = ifelse(runif(2000) < 0.8, summer, 1 - summer)`). How much of the confounding comes back? (Measurement error makes "we controlled for it" a matter of degree.) ::: ::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"} # Advanced - Find the collider in your own data. Name a dataset you have worked with whose rows exist because they cleared a bar --hired, admitted, published, survived, responded. Draw its DAG, simulate a world with the same selection rule, and show how large a Berkson bias it could put into the relationship you actually care about. ::: ## Key takeaways - Every causal structure is built from three atoms: fork (confounder), chain (mediator), collider. - Adjusting for a confounder removes bias; adjusting for a collider *creates* it -- the same action, opposite effect, depending on the atom. - Whether to adjust for a variable is not a statistical question: only your DAG -- your drawn assumptions -- can answer it. - If your data was filtered before you got it (hired, admitted, published, survived), collider bias may already be in it. ::: {.continue-learning} [← Previous: All models are wrong](/sessions_thinking/03-regression/03-regression.qmd) [Track overview: Think with data →](/learn/thinking.qmd) [Next: Earning the arrow →](/sessions_thinking/05-designs/05-designs.qmd) :::
